Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the SolarNova Energy Q3 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. Instructions for those wishing to ask a question will be provided at that time. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss SolarNova Energy's results for the Q3. Joining me on today's call are Jordan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Taylor Brooks, Chief Financial Officer; and Morgan Lee, Chief Development Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call will contain forward-looking statements. We encourage you to review the disclaimer in our press release and on our website regarding these statements.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Jordan Hale.

Jordan Hale:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. SolarNova Energy delivered a solid performance in the Q3, driven by strong execution and growing demand for our renewable energy solutions. We are making significant progress on our strategic priorities, including expanding our project pipeline, enhancing our technological capabilities, and strengthening our partnerships.

I'd like to highlight four key aspects of our performance this quarter. First, the favorable policy and regulatory environment that's accelerating our growth. Second, our capacity addition guidance and robust pipeline targets. Third, the new PPAs we've secured along with strong average PPA pricing. And fourth, the continued positive trends in our gross and operating margins.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Taylor Brooks to discuss these in more detail, along with our financial results.

Taylor Brooks:
Thank you, Jordan, and good morning, everyone. Before we open the line for Q&A, I'd like to provide some color on the policy and regulatory landscape, which continues to be a major tailwind for SolarNova Energy as we execute on our 40 GW pipeline of utility-scale solar and storage projects. Our team has been laser-focused on navigating this dynamic environment, and I'm pleased to report that supportive policies across key markets are accelerating deployment timelines and enhancing project IRRs by an average of 150-200 basis points year-over-year.

Starting domestically in the U.S., the Inflation Reduction Act—or IRA—remains the cornerstone of our growth strategy. Since its passage in August 2022, the IRA has catalyzed over $300 billion in announced clean energy investments, with solar and storage capturing roughly 45% of that, per recent EIA data. For us specifically, the enhanced 30% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) with its 10% domestic content adder and 10% energy community bonus has boosted our after-tax yields on greenfield projects to north of 12%. Take our 1.2 GW Texas portfolio, for instance: by sourcing 45% of our bifacial PERC modules and racking from U.S. facilities—partnering with First Solar and our own Nevada fab—we qualified for the full adder stack, reducing effective CAPEX by 18% compared to pre-IRA bids.

That said, we're not blind to headwinds. Interconnection queues remain a bottleneck, with FERC's Order No. 2020 aiming to clear backlogs by prioritizing "ready-to-build" projects like ours, which feature co-located BESS with 4-hour duration at 80% capacity factors. We've seen cluster study reforms shave 6-9 months off timelines in PJM and ERCOT, but SPP and MISO still lag. On the state level, California's NEM 3.0 rollout has tempered rooftop solar growth—down 25% YoY per SEIA stats—but it's driving hyperscaler demand for utility-scale PPAs, where we've locked in 2.5 GW at $35/MWh fixed through 2030 with Google and Microsoft. Looking ahead, with the election cycle heating up, we're modeling a 10-15% risk discount on IRA extensions, but our diversified 60/40 utility-scale/rooftop mix and $2.5 billion undrawn credit facility position us resiliently.

Shifting to Europe, the REPowerEU plan and EU Green Deal are firing on all cylinders post-Ukraine, targeting 45% renewables by 2030. This has unlocked €300 billion in subsidies via the Innovation Fund and Recovery Facility, with solar auctions yielding record-low LCOEs of €22/MWh in Spain's latest round—down 15% YoY. Our 800 MW portfolio in Iberia and Italy benefits directly: we've secured CfDs under Portugal's simplified auction framework at €25/MWh, with 200 MWh/4-hour lithium-iron-phosphate storage to capture peak pricing under the Electricity Market Design reforms. The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), effective from 2026, is a strategic boon—our Warsaw-listed Polish JV now produces TOPCon modules with 22.5% efficiency, fully EU-sourced to dodge the 20-35% carbon tariffs on Asian imports.

Challenges persist, however. Germany's EEG surcharge phase-out has squeezed merchant revenues, prompting us to hybridize 70% of our projects with intraday trading via EPEX Spot. Permitting harmonization under the Net-Zero Industry Act should cut approval times from 18 months to under 12 by Q4 2025, aligning with our 1.5 GW shovel-ready queue. We're also eyeing the U.K.'s CfD Allocation Round 6, where our Humber Gateway offshore-hybrid tender—pairing 500 MW floating solar with Orsted's wind—positions us for £50/MWh strikes.

In Asia-Pacific, China's dominance in the supply chain—producing 95% of global polysilicon and 80% of cells—continues to pressure module ASPs to $0.22/W, a 30% drop since 2023. But Beijing's 1,200 GW wind+solar target by 2030, backed by the 14th Five-Year Plan's R&D subsidies, has stabilized domestic demand. For SolarNova, our Shanghai manufacturing outpost supplies 60% of our APAC projects, qualifying for the 20% VAT rebate and navigating Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act compliance via blockchain-traced ingots. India's Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme is a standout: our 2 GW Rajasthan thin-film fab, modeled after Adani Green, taps ₹24,000 crore in allocations, targeting 25% module cost savings and export credits to the U.S. under IRA's transferability rules.

Emerging markets add upside. Australia's Rewiring the Nation fund has fast-tracked our 400 MW Queensland BESS, with AEMO's Integrated System Plan forecasting 28 GW storage by 2030. In LATAM, Brazil's Proinfa auctions awarded us 300 MW at R$140/MWh, bolstered by BNDES green financing at SOFR+150bps.

Strategically, we're de-risking via three pillars: First, localization—scaling U.S. and EU capacity to 10 GW annually by 2026 to capture adders and CBAM shields, mirroring Enphase's fab expansions. Second, policy advocacy—as a SEIA board member and RE100 participant, we're pushing FERC 2025 reforms and EU permitting fast-tracks, with $15 million allocated to lobbying. Third, financial innovation—monetizing tax credits via PTC/ITC transfers, generating $450 million in Q3 liquidity alone, akin to our deals with JPMorgan. This has our forward EBITDA margins expanding to 28-30%, with ROIC hitting 11% on the back of 25% YoY backlog growth to $18 billion.

In summary, the regulatory tide is unequivocally rising for clean tech. While volatility persists—think U.S. elections or EU budget wrangles—our execution playbook, blending policy capture with tech leadership in n-type TOPCon and long-duration flow batteries, leaves us ahead of the curve. We're raising our 2025 guidance by 10% to 8.5 GW deployed, confident in delivering shareholder value.

Turning now to our capacity addition guidance and pipeline targets, which remain the cornerstone of our multi-year growth story at SolarNova Energy. For those new to our calls, we are a leading independent power producer focused on utility-scale solar PV, onshore wind, battery energy storage systems—or BESS—and emerging hybrid solutions, with a portfolio spanning North America, Europe, and select APAC markets.

Let me start with a quick recap of where we stand today. As of September 30th, year-to-date, we've achieved 2.7 GW of nameplate capacity additions across our backlog, bringing our operating portfolio to 13.3 GW globally. This includes the COD of our 450 MWdc Ironwood Solar project in ERCOT, Texas—our largest single-site bifacial PV installation to date, utilizing high-efficiency TOPCon modules from LONGi and paired with a 200 MWh Tesla Megapack BESS for firming. Year-over-year, our additions are up 25%, driven by favorable module pricing trends—global spot prices for mono PERC modules have fallen to around $0.22/W—and accelerated permitting under the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act, or IRA.

Turning to guidance: For full-year 2024, we are reaffirming our capacity addition target of 4.2–4.5 GW, weighted 65% toward solar PV, 20% wind, and 15% standalone and co-located BESS. This represents a 22% increase over 2023's 3.5 GW. Breaking it down by quarter: Q4 will see ~1.2 GW online, anchored by the 650 MWdc Desert Bloom hybrid in California's CAISO market—solar plus 300 MWh flow battery storage from Form Energy—and our 300 MW onshore wind repower in PJM, upgrading Vestas V90 turbines to V150-4.2 MW platforms for a 40% capacity uplift. The year closes strong with prior quarters' momentum carrying forward.

Looking further out, our 2025 guidance is 7.5–8.0 GW in additions—a 75% ramp from 2024—fueled by a maturing backlog and $15 billion in secured project financing. By technology: Solar remains dominant at 55% or ~4.2 GW, with a shift toward larger 1 GW+ clusters using heterojunction or HJT modules to chase sub-$25/MWh LCOE in sunny markets. Wind jumps to 25% or 2 GW, emphasizing high-yield sites in the U.S. Midwest and Iberia. BESS surges to 20% or 1.6 GW/4.8 GWh, reflecting grid operator mandates like ERCOT's 5.5 GW blackstart requirements and MISO's 10 GW storage queue priority. Hybrids, including solar-wind-storage and nascent green hydrogen pilots, make up the balance.

Our pipeline underpins this with exceptional visibility. We maintain a 48 GW late-stage pipeline—defined as projects past Notice to Proceed or NTP, with PPAs executed and >80% EPC contracted—and a 120 GW early-to-mid-stage funnel, up 15% QoQ and 35% YoY. This positions us for 10+ GW annual additions by 2027, targeting a 20–25% CAGR through the decade.

Let me unpack the pipeline regionally and technologically for clarity:

North America (75% of late-stage, 65% of total pipeline: 36 GW late, 78 GW total)  
The U.S. is our growth engine, with 28 GW late-stage. IRA tax credits—PTC/ITC at 30–50% with adders for domestic content (we're at 25% U.S.-sourced modules via First Solar partnerships) and energy communities—have de-risked economics, yielding IRRs north of 12% even at 7% WACC. ERCOT leads with 12 GW late-stage, including 2.5 GW of shovel-ready solar+BESS hybrids targeting merchant exposure amid projected 2025 price spikes from data center load growth (hello, hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft). PJM and SPP follow with 8 GW combined, where we're prioritizing interconnection queue reforms—post-FERC Order 2023, we've fast-tracked 15 GW out of the 2,500 GW U.S. queue. Canada adds 2 GW via Alberta's renewables push. Risks here include interest rate sensitivity—every 50 bps Fed hike shaves 1–2% off unlevered IRRs—but our fixed-rate debt (avg. 4.8% all-in) and 70% hedged PPAs mitigate this.

Europe (15% late-stage, 20% total: 7.2 GW late, 24 GW total)  
REPowerEU's 600 GW non-fossil target by 2030 has unlocked €200B+ in subsidies. Our 4 GW Iberian late-stage pipeline—Spain/Portugal—features 1.2 GW floating solar on reservoirs, partnering with BayWa r.e., with LCOE at €25/MWh thanks to 25-year CfD auctions. UK rounds out with 1.5 GW onshore wind extensions under Contracts for Difference at £50/MWh, navigating planning delays via our dedicated policy team. Germany contributes 1.3 GW solar, but EEG surcharge reforms have tempered merchant upside. We're eyeing 5 GW expansion into Poland's Baltic offshore wind auctions.

APAC and Emerging (10% late-stage, 15% total: 4.8 GW late, 18 GW total)  
India's 500 GW non-fossil goal by 2030 drives our 2 GW late-stage Rajasthan solar cluster, with SECI PPAs at INR 2.5/kWh (~$0.03/kWh) using 600W+ tunnel oxide passivated contact modules. Australia's 82% renewables by 2030 NEM targets yield 1.8 GW, including our 500 MWdc+250 MWh BESS in Queensland. We're piloting 500 MW green hydrogen via electrolyzers in India, tied to our solar offtake, with offtake from Adani and NTPC.

Strategically, we're laser-focused on three initiatives to execute this pipeline:

1. Technology Roadmap: Transitioning 40% of 2025 solar to n-type TOPCon/HJT for 24–26% efficiencies, reducing BoS costs by 15%. BESS fleet averages 4-hour duration, with 20% long-duration (8+ hours) via iron-air tech. Wind fleet modernizes to 15 MW offshore platforms, akin to Orsted's Hornsea scale.

2. Commercial Innovation: 85% of late-stage backed by investment-grade PPAs—50% utility, 30% corporate (e.g., Google's 1 GW global deal framework), 20% merchant/sleeved. Hybrid co-location boosts capacity factors to 35–45%, capturing ancillary services revenue (e.g., $100/kW-yr freq response in CAISO).

3. Execution Excellence: $2.5B liquidity supports 10 GW FIDs in 2025. Supply chain secured via 10 GW module offtake with JinkoSolar/Trina, hedging 80% poly-Si exposure amid Xinjiang bans. Permitting velocity up 30% via AI-driven siting tools and local stakeholder programs.

In summary, our guidance and pipeline reflect disciplined growth amid tailwinds like 15% YoY global module cost declines, 20% capex reductions per GW, and policy momentum. We expect FY24 EBITDA of $1.8–2.0B on these additions, with ROIC expanding to 10% by 2026. We're well-positioned to outperform peers like NextEra or Invenergy, trading at a premium multiple for our 4x backlog-to-build ratio.

Next, I'll turn to our commercial progress, specifically the strength of our PPA backlog and pricing dynamics, which remain a cornerstone of our long-term revenue visibility in this capital-intensive industry.

I'm thrilled to report that in Q3, we secured 1.8 GW of new PPAs across our development pipeline, bringing our total locked-in contracted capacity to over 12 GW through 2030. This represents a 45% quarter-over-quarter increase in new bookings and marks our strongest quarter for PPA executions since Q1 2022. These agreements span both utility-scale solar-plus-storage projects and standalone wind assets, underscoring our diversified technology stack.

Breaking it down by key deals:
- Our flagship 850 MW solar-plus-storage PPA in the ERCOT market with TexSun Energy, a repeat counterparty. This 15-year fixed-price agreement includes 200 MWh of 4-hour lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) storage, priced with a capacity performance adjustment to capture peak summer demand. Deployment is slated for H2 2026, leveraging our proprietary DC-coupled system that boosts round-trip efficiency to 92%—well above the industry average of 85-88%.
- A 650 MW bifacial PERC-plus wind-solar hybrid PPA with Amazon Web Services, part of their aggressive 100% RE100 commitment. This 20-year deal in CAISO features high-efficiency N-type TOPCon modules from partners like LONGi and Trina Solar, paired with single-axis trackers from Array Technologies, yielding a projected capacity factor of 32%—a 15% uplift from our legacy portfolio.
- Smaller but strategically vital: 300 MW of distributed solar PPAs across PJM and MISO with corporate off-takers like Microsoft and Procter & Gamble, emphasizing virtual power purchase agreements (VPPAs) with green attributes certified under RECs and GO Certificates.

Regionally, 65% of new PPAs are U.S.-based, capitalizing on the IRA's PTC/ITC extensions and the queue acceleration in ERCOT and SPP, where interconnection timelines have compressed to under 24 months thanks to RTO reforms. We've also inked 25% in Europe (primarily Spain and Italy under REPowerEU incentives), where TSOs like REE are fast-tracking grid upgrades, and 10% in Australia, hedging against NEM oversupply via firming with our BESS co-location strategy. This geographic mix mitigates risks from U.S. election-year policy uncertainty and Europe's nuclear phase-out dynamics.

On pricing, our blended average PPA price for new contracts came in at $38.50 per MWh, a 12% premium to Q2's $34.20/MWh and up 8% year-over-year. This resilience bucks the broader trend of PPA prices softening 5-10% in merchant-heavy markets like ERCOT due to record solar buildouts—over 20 GW expected online in 2024 per EIA data. Our outperformance stems from:
- Inflation escalators averaging 2.5% annually, tied to CPI-U, which have preserved real yields amid sticky input costs for polysilicon and EPC labor.
- Value-stacking: Merchant tail options on 30% of capacity allow upside from ancillary services like frequency regulation, adding $4-6/MWh in expected revenue.
- Storage carve-outs: PPAs with dispatchable profiles command 20-25% premiums over pure solar/wind, aligning with FERC Order 2222 enabling DER aggregation.

Strategically, these PPAs de-risk our $2.5 billion development capex runway, securing 85% of our 5-year EBITDA at an average IRR of 11.2% post-tax credits. We're proactively addressing merchant volatility—now at 15-20% of our operating fleet—by layering in more corporate VPPAs, which grew 30% QoQ amid Big Tech's Scope 2 decarbonization mandates. Looking ahead, our 5 GW late-stage pipeline at an average implied price of $36/MWh positions us for continued backlog growth, even as LCOE for utility-scale solar dips below $25/MWh in sunny IRRs like the Southwest.

This commercial momentum validates our tech-forward approach: investing in AI-optimized O&M platforms akin to those from Enverus or Stem, which have lifted fleet availability to 98.5%. We'll provide full PPA disclosures in our 10-Q, including shape factors and clawback provisions.

Finally, on our gross margin and operating margin performance, which continue to reflect the structural improvements we're driving across our solar module manufacturing, utility-scale energy storage systems, and offshore wind turbine components. As you know, SolarNova Energy has been laser-focused on operational leverage in this high-growth Clean Tech landscape, where we're benefiting from the tailwinds of the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), Europe's REPowerEU initiative, and surging global demand for baseload renewables amid the energy transition.

Starting with gross margins, we delivered a Q3 gross margin of 29.8%, up 450 basis points year-over-year from 25.3% and 110 basis points sequentially from Q2's 28.7%. This marks our sixth consecutive quarter of gross margin expansion, bringing our trailing four-quarter average to 27.6%—well above our long-term target of 25-28% and positioning us competitively against peers like First Solar, which reported around 26-28% in their recent quarters, or Enphase Energy in the inverter space at similar levels.

Several factors drove this outperformance. First, cost deflation in our bill of materials (BOM): Polysilicon spot prices, which peaked at over $40/kg last year, have stabilized around $10-12/kg, directly benefiting our TOPCon (Tunnel Oxide Passivated Contact) solar modules, where silicon accounts for ~40% of COGS. We've locked in forward contracts with key suppliers like Tongwei and GCL-Poly, hedging ~70% of our 2024 needs at favorable rates. Silver paste costs, another pain point, fell 15% QoQ due to our strategic shift to thinner wire metallization tech, reducing usage by 20 grams per module without efficiency loss—our Gen-3 TOPCon panels now hit 24.5% conversion efficiency, rivaling LONGi's latest Hi-MO 6 offerings.

Second, manufacturing scale and yield improvements: Our U.S. Fab 3 in Ohio, incentivized by $500M+ in IRA Section 45X tax credits, ramped to 80% utilization in Q3, up from 55% a year ago. This drove fixed cost absorption, with module COGS dropping to $0.22/W—our lowest ever and 15% below the global c-Si average per IRENA benchmarks. Yields on n-type TOPCon lines exceeded 98%, thanks to AI-optimized plasma etching processes that cut defect rates by 30%. In energy storage, our LFP battery packs saw gross margins expand to 32% from 27%, driven by vertical integration with our Nevada gigafactory, where we're now producing 80% of our BESS cells in-house, mitigating tariff risks from Asian imports.

Regionally, U.S. deployments—now 45% of revenue—delivered outsized margins at 32%, fueled by IRA-driven PPAs with utilities like NextEra and Duke Energy. Europe, at 30% of mix, held steady at 28% despite softer module prices from Chinese oversupply, offset by our premium bifacial trackers commanding €0.35/W premiums. APAC faced headwinds, with margins at 24% due to intense competition from Trina Solar and Jinko, but we're pivoting to higher-margin O&M services there.

Turning to operating margins, we achieved 14.2% in Q3, a robust 380 bps YoY improvement from 10.4% and up 90 bps QoQ. This brings our T4Q operating margin to 12.9%, approaching our 13-15% aspirational range. The expansion was propelled by gross margin leverage, coupled with disciplined OpEx control: SG&A as a percentage of revenue dipped to 8.2% from 9.5% YoY, reflecting workforce optimization post our 2023 restructuring, while R&D held at 4.1% of sales—invested in next-gen HJT (Heterojunction Technology) pilots and solid-state battery prototypes targeting 500 Wh/kg densities by 2026.

Key strategic levers here include supply chain localization: 65% of our U.S. content now qualifies for full IRA bonuses, reducing landed costs by 12% vs. imports and shielding us from Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act scrutiny. We're also advancing module recycling initiatives, with our Arizona facility processing 50 MW of EOL panels quarterly, generating $5M in circular revenue streams at 40% margins—early proof of our closed-loop ESG strategy, aligning with EU Battery Regulation mandates.

Challenges persist: Wind segment margins compressed to 22% gross due to steel price volatility (up 10% on Red Sea disruptions) and turbine curtailment risks in the North Sea, but our partnership with Ørsted on 1 GW fixed-bottom projects is yielding Vestas-comparable nacelle efficiencies.

Looking forward, we guide Q4 gross margins to 30-31%, with full-year at 29.5%, assuming stable commodity inputs and 20% volume growth to 8 GW modules shipped. Operating margins should hit 14.5-15.5% for Q4, scaling to 15%+ in FY25 as Fab 4 comes online in Texas. Risks include potential ASP erosion if Chinese dumping intensifies, but our premium tech stack—TOPCon-to-HJT roadmap—and backlog of 15 GW (65% contracted) provide strong visibility.

These trends underscore SolarNova's transformation into a high-margin, U.S.-centric leader in the $1.7T global renewables market, per BloombergNEF. We're not just riding the wave; we're engineering the efficiency gains that will sustain 20%+ EPS CAGR through the decade.

As Jordan mentioned, we had a strong financial performance in the Q3. Our revenue was $620 million, representing a 42% increase year-over-year. This growth was primarily driven by increased project commissioning and higher energy production across our portfolio. Our gross margin was 29.8%, reflecting improved operational efficiency and favorable pricing. Operating expenses were $180 million, primarily due to increased investments in research and development and sales and marketing. Our net income was $95 million, or $0.72 per share. We ended the quarter with $1.8 billion in cash and cash equivalents. We are reaffirming our full-year guidance for revenue and earnings.

Now, I'll turn the call back to Jordan for closing remarks.

Jordan Hale:
Thank you, Taylor. In closing, I am confident that SolarNova Energy is well-positioned to capitalize on the growing demand for renewable energy. We remain focused on executing our strategic priorities and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.

Operator, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Instructions for the question-and-answer session. Our first question comes from Chris Patel with Greenlight Capital. Please go ahead.

Chris Patel:
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of your new n-type TOPCon modules on your project economics?

Jordan Hale:
Good morning, Chris. Absolutely, our n-type TOPCon modules are transforming our project economics across the board. As Taylor highlighted, these modules are achieving 24-26% efficiencies, which directly translates to higher capacity factors—up to 32% in hybrids like our CAISO deals—and lower LCOE targets below $25/MWh in prime solar regions. Compared to our legacy PERC tech, they've reduced BoS costs by 15% through better performance ratios and minimized degradation, boosting unlevered IRRs by 150-200 bps. In our ERCOT and Southwest portfolios, this stacks beautifully with IRA adders for domestic content, where we're hitting 25% U.S. sourcing, pushing after-tax yields over 12%. We've already deployed them in the Ironwood project, where they contributed to a 92% round-trip efficiency in DC-coupled storage setups. Looking ahead, as we transition 40% of 2025 solar additions to TOPCon/HJT, expect even stronger merchant upside from ancillary services and value-stacking. It's a key differentiator in our 48 GW late-stage pipeline.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Sarah Kim with EcoInvest Partners. Please go ahead.

Sarah Kim:
What are your expectations for grid connection timelines for your upcoming projects?

Morgan Lee:
Good morning, Sarah. Grid connection timelines are improving markedly thanks to regulatory reforms. In the U.S., FERC Order 2020 and cluster study changes have shaved 6-9 months off in PJM and ERCOT, with our ready-to-build solar+BESS hybrids—featuring 4-hour duration at 80% capacity factors—prioritized out of the massive queues. We're modeling 24 months or less for our 12 GW ERCOT late-stage, down from 36+ pre-reform. In Europe, Net-Zero Industry Act harmonization should cut permitting to under 12 months by Q4 2025 for our 7.2 GW pipeline, while REPowerEU fast-tracks TSO upgrades in Iberia. Australia and India are even faster, with AEMO and SECI approvals in 12-18 months for our NEM and Rajasthan clusters. We've fast-tracked 15 GW via reforms, supported by AI siting and policy advocacy. Overall, this supports our 4.2-4.5 GW FY24 additions and 7.5-8 GW in 2025 without delays.

Operator:
Instructions for the question-and-answer session. There appear to be no further questions at this time. I will now turn the call back over to Jordan Hale for any closing remarks.

Jordan Hale:
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. We appreciate your interest in SolarNova Energy. We look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
